dasornis:enwiki:6.title: Dasornis (Other fossils perhaps belonging in Dasornis)

facts.statement: Most Dasornis fossils date to approximately 50 million years ago and were found in the Early Eocene London Clay of the Isle of Sheppey in England.
facts.quote: Almost all known material of this bird is from some 50 million years ago (Ma) and has been recovered from the Ypresian (Early Eocene) London Clay of the Isle of Sheppey (England).

facts.statement: A few tentatively assigned Dasornis remains from approximately 45 million years ago were found in the Middle Eocene of Etterbeek, Belgium.
facts.quote: The exception are a few approximately 45 Ma-old remains from the Lutetian (Middle Eocene, MP11-13) of Etterbeek (Belgium) that are only tentatively included here

facts.statement: Dasornis is classified in the order Odontopterygiformes due to uncertainty regarding its closest relatives.
facts.quote: they are placed in the order Odontopterygiformes to account for this uncertainty.

facts.statement: Dasornis was a huge bird with a wingspan exceeding 5 meters and possibly reaching 6 meters.
facts.quote: This genus belongs to the group of huge pseudotooth birds, with wingspans in excess of 5 m, and probably as much as 6 m.

facts.statement: The complete head and bill of Dasornis measured almost 45 centimeters in life.
facts.quote: The complete head and bill probably measured almost 45 cm in life

facts.statement: Dasornis had an eye socket diameter of 55 millimeters and a humerus distal end width of about 35 millimeters.
facts.quote: the eye socket had a diameter of 55 mm and the humerus at its distal end was about 35 mm wide.

facts.statement: The first fossil of Dasornis emuinus, a right humerus shaft, was found in the Isle of Sheppey and misidentified as a paleognath bone by James Scott Bowerbank in 1854.
facts.quote: The first fossil of D. emuinus, a piece of right humerus shaft, was found in the Ypresian (Early Eocene) London Clay of the Isle of Sheppey (England). It was misidentified as a tibiotarsus of the paleognath Lithornis and described as L. emuinus by James Scott Bowerbank in 1854.

facts.statement: Richard Owen established the genus Dasornis in 1870 based on a broken skull found in the same deposits as the first specimen.
facts.quote: Richard Owen established the genera Dasornis (in 1870) and Argillornis (in 1878) for, respectively, a broken skull and two humerus ends that were found in the same deposits.

facts.statement: A well-preserved skull lacking the beak was discovered in the Isle of Sheppey London Clay at the start of the 21st century.
facts.quote: Almost 150 years after the description of "L." emuinus, at the start of the 21st century, a rather well-preserved skull (lacking the beak) was discovered, once again in the Isle of Sheppey London Clay.

facts.statement: The current valid name Dasornis emuinus combines the oldest valid genus and species names used for these fossils.
facts.quote: Dasornis emuinus applies, a novel combination of the oldest valid genus and species names ever used for these fossils.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Dasornis was restricted to the North Atlantic and Paratethys or also occurred in the Pacific and Southern Hemisphere.
facts.quote: it is not at all clear whether the genus was restricted to the North Atlantic (and perhaps the adjacent Paratethys) or occurred also in the Pacific and in the Southern Hemisphere, where fossils of a similar size were found

facts.statement: The genus Dasornis includes several junior synonyms such as Argillornis, Dasyornis, Megalornis, and Neptuniavis.
facts.quote: The junior synonyms of the genus Dasornis are thus: Argillornis Owen, 1878 "Dasornis" Owen, 1869 (nomen nudum) Dasyornis Lydekker, 1891 (non Vigors & Horsfield, 1836: preoccupied) Megalornis Seeley, 1866 (non Gray, 1841: preoccupied) Neptuniavis Harrison & C.A.Walker, 1977

facts.statement: The species Dasornis emuinus has numerous junior synonyms including Argillornis emuinus, Megalornis emuinus, and Odontopteryx.
facts.quote: The junior synonyms of the species D. emuinus are: Argillornis emuinus (Bowerbank, 1854) Argillornis longipennis Owen, 1878 Argillornis longipes Lambrecht, 1933 (lapsus) "Dasornis londinensis" Owen, 1869 (nomen nudum) Dasornis londinensis Owen, 1870 Dasornis londiniensis Lydekker, 1891 (unjustified emendation) Lithornis emuinus Bowerbank, 1854 Megalornis emuianus Seeley, 1866 (lapsus) Megalornis emuinus Lambrecht, 1921 (lapsus) Neptuniavis miranda Harrison & C.A.Walker, 1977 Odontopteryx Owen, 1873

facts.statement: A fossil named "Pseudodontornis" longidentata, found in the Early Eocene London Clay of the Isle of Sheppey, may be synonymous with Dasornis emuinus.
facts.quote: "Pseudodontornis" longidentata, described from a beak piece and a damaged atlas vertebra of what appears to have been a single individual, is yet another supposed pseudotooth bird species from the Early Eocene London Clay of the Isle of Sheppey.

facts.statement: Middle Eocene fossils from Etterbeek, Belgium, originally assigned to Argillornis might belong to Dasornis.
facts.quote: This also applies to the Lutetian (Middle Eocene) material from Etterbeek (Belgium) which was at first assigned to Argillornis

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that Gigantornis, known from a sternum in Middle Eocene rocks in Nigeria, could belong to the genus Dasornis.
facts.quote: Perhaps Gigantornis which is only known from pieces of a sternum found in Middle Eocene rocks in Nigeria also belongs in Dasornis

facts.statement: Unidentified large pelagornithid fossils from the Middle Eocene of Togo, provisionally named "Aequornis traversei", may help clarify the classification of Dasornis.
facts.quote: Analysis of the unidentified large pelagornithid fossils from the Middle Eocene of Kpogamé-Hahotoé (Togo) which are provisionally termed "Aequornis traversei" might shed light on this issue.

facts.statement: Large undescribed remains from the Late Paleocene/Early Eocene of Morocco, termed "Odontopteryx gigas", might actually be from a small or juvenile Dasornis.
facts.quote: The fairly large undescribed remains from the Late Paleocene/Early Eocene of the Ouled Abdoun Basin (Morocco) which have been provisionally termed "Odontopteryx gigas" may in fact be from a small or juvenile Dasornis.

facts.statement: It is undetermined whether Pacific pelagornithid fossils from Oregon are the same species as Atlantic Dasornis emuinus, but age differences suggest they may belong to different genera.
facts.quote: Whether this Pacific species was the same as the Atlantic D. emuinus is undetermined, but considering the age difference it is not all too likely and they may well belong to different genera.

facts.statement: Fossil remains from Antarctica, including a jaw piece from Seymour Island and a humerus from Mount Discovery, are similar in size and age to Dasornis but are too fragmentary to be confidently assigned to it.
facts.quote: Similar in size and age to the present genus are some pseudotooth bird remains from Antarctica, namely a jaw piece from the Middle/Late Eocene of the La Meseta Formation of Seymour Island near the Drake Passage, and a Middle Eocene piece of a humerus shaft from Mount Discovery on the continent's Pacific side.

facts.statement: Dasornis belongs to the parent group Pelagornithidae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Pelagornithidae

facts.statement: Dasornis is classified within the family Pelagornithidae.
facts.quote: Family: Pelagornithidae

facts.statement: Dasornis lived from the Selandian to the Priabonian stages, between 61.66 and 33.9 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Selandian to Priabonian (61.66 to 33.9 million years ago)

facts.statement: There are 24 recorded fossil occurrences of Dasornis in the Paleobiology Database.
facts.quote: Fossil occurrences recorded: 24
